blocks.text: 1. Adaptive RAG

blocks.alt: A query goes through a complexity classifier that routes by complexity

blocks.text: Self-RAG closed by weighing when its training requirement is worth it. Adaptive RAG, which chooses a different pipeline strategy per query, closes out the middle stretch of the advanced RAG family by combining ideas from every pattern covered so far.
It classifies query complexity first, then routes to the matching strategy, a classification and routing technique explored in full throughout this topic.
2. One Strategy Does Not Fit Every Query
A single fixed pipeline, like the baseline covered in Naive RAG, either over-invests in simple queries or under-invests in complex ones.
Adaptive RAG matches the strategy to the actual query instead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Query complexity","Matched strategy"],"rows":[["Simple","Skip retrieval entirely"],["Moderate","Single retrieval and generation pass"],["Complex","Multi-step retrieval or decomposition"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Classifying Query Complexity First

blocks.alt: A query goes through a classifier to produce a complexity level

blocks.text: A lightweight classifier labels each incoming query as simple, moderate, or complex.
That label then determines which pipeline path the query takes.
4. Simple Queries Skip Retrieval Entirely

blocks.alt: A simple query gets a direct answer with no retrieval

blocks.text: Similar to the retrieval decision covered in Self-RAG, a simple query the model can already answer confidently skips retrieval altogether.
This saves the latency and cost of an unnecessary search.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query like what is two plus two never needs a retrieval call at all, and routing it straight to generation avoids paying for a search the model did not need.

blocks.text: 5. Moderate Queries Use A Single Retrieval Pass

blocks.alt: A moderate query uses a single retrieval pass

blocks.text: A moderate query routes through the standard single retrieval and generation pipeline.
This is the same flow already covered in Naive RAG.
6. Complex Queries Trigger Multi-Step Retrieval

blocks.alt: A complex query triggers multi-step retrieval

blocks.text: Much as multi-hop questions benefit most from step by step reasoning in Chain Of Thought, a complex query routes through multiple retrieval rounds or decomposition.
This pays the added latency only where it is actually needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","Latency cost"],"rows":[["Skip retrieval","Lowest, no search at all"],["Single pass","Moderate, one search and one generation"],["Multi-step","Highest, but only paid when actually needed"]]}

blocks.text: 7. The Complexity Classifier Needs Its Own Training

blocks.alt: The complexity classifier requires its own training

blocks.text: Much like the grader model covered in Corrective RAG, the complexity classifier is typically trained on labeled query examples.
A misclassified query routes to the wrong strategy entirely.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A complex query mistakenly classified as simple skips retrieval it actually needed, producing a confident but ungrounded answer instead of the correct multi-step lookup.

blocks.text: 8. Adaptive RAG Builds On Modular RAG
Building on the routing between modules covered in Modular RAG, adaptive RAG is essentially a routing layer choosing between naive, single pass, and multi-step module combinations.
It is a concrete application of that general modular routing idea.
9. Recognizing When Adaptive RAG Earns Its Classifier Overhead

blocks.alt: Widely varying query complexity points toward adaptive RAG

blocks.text: A system facing a wide mix of query difficulty benefits most from adaptive routing.
A system facing uniformly similar queries, by contrast, rarely needs per-query classification.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a fixed pipeline for every query instead of classifying complexity first.
Training the complexity classifier on too narrow a set of example queries.
Routing a misclassified complex query to the cheaper simple path and getting an ungrounded answer.
Adding adaptive routing to a workload where every query already has similar complexity.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Adaptive RAG classifies query complexity first, then routes to a matching strategy.
A single fixed pipeline either over-invests in simple queries or under-invests in complex ones.
A lightweight classifier labels each query as simple, moderate, or complex.
Simple queries skip retrieval entirely, saving the cost of an unnecessary search.
Moderate queries use the standard single retrieval and generation pipeline.
Complex queries trigger multi-step retrieval or decomposition, paying latency only where needed.
The complexity classifier itself needs training, and a misclassification routes to the wrong strategy.
Adaptive RAG is essentially a routing layer built on modular RAG's general routing idea.
This closes naive, corrective, self, and adaptive RAG as the core self-correcting patterns; Fusion RAG covers combining multiple retrieval results next.
